intro: A viola string-crossing exercise becomes a lyrical portrait. The tune’s leaps have a physical source in the movement of a bow from string to string.
question: How does a technical exercise become an expressive melody?

sections.label: VI · A viola exercise transformed
sections.mNote: wide intervals connect the exercise with the lyrical line

cues.title: A bow crosses strings
cues.text: The viola’s opening figure crosses between strings. Listen across the variation for the contrast between that separated, leaping motion and the more connected melody that grows from it.
cues.evidence: Novello pp. 31–34, rehearsal figures 19–22; Elgar describes the opening as an exercise in crossing strings. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigma_Variations
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Isabel Fitton’s instrument
cues.text: “Ysobel” is Isabel Fitton, an amateur viola player from a Malvern musical family. The chosen instrument belongs to the person being remembered, not merely to a convenient orchestral colour.
cues.evidence: The Elgar Society identifies Fitton and her instrument. https://elgar.org/3enigma.htm

cues.title: The later swell recedes
cues.text: After the later swell, the sound diminishes towards the short ending. Keep the viola’s leaping shape in mind while the accompaniment gives back its weight.
cues.evidence: The report peaks around 0:40–0:45 and drops at 0:50, reaching a low level by 1:00. This supports a closing withdrawal, not a precise solo entry.

source.title: Elgar, Enigma Variations, full score (Novello)
source.locator: PDF pp. 31–34, rehearsal figures 19–22. Whole-variation passage map; the report’s changes around 0:12, 0:22, 0:40 and 0:50 support the succession from exposed viola to fuller phrases and a quiet close.

timeline.note: Viola string-crossing is exposed over restrained support; the initial very soft low-brass chord belongs to the link from the preceding variation (p. 31).
Flutes and horns enter the growing phrase; bassoon figures answer the viola’s shape (pp. 31–32).
The middle phrase keeps the lower string voices exposed, with small wind responses rather than heavy brass (p. 32).
The later swell broadens the string line and adds wind colour around it (p. 33; the report’s strongest span).
The closing string and wind gestures diminish; horn support remains restrained and the large brass is silent (p. 34).

facts: Largely self-taught; violin, organ, orchestral playing and his father’s Worcester music shop
Bandmaster, Worcester County Asylum, Powick, 1879–84 · organist, St George’s Catholic Church, 1885–89 · Master of the King’s Musick, 1924–34
Two completed symphonies; violin and cello concertos; choral works; chamber music; five completed Pomp and Circumstance marches
composer.background:
Elgar learned the orchestra from inside it. His father William kept a music shop in Worcester, tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church. Edward read the scores in the shop, played violin in local ensembles, taught several instruments and eventually succeeded his father at the organ. He was born in Lower Broadheath in 1857, a Catholic in a predominantly Anglican musical establishment and a tradesman’s son in a profession increasingly organised around London colleges. He remained sensitive to both distinctions throughout his later success. His practical education taught him how a phrase feels under a bow.

At Powick he wrote quadrilles and polkas for an unusual ensemble, learning to give each instrument useful work. The Three Choirs Festival brought larger repertory within reach: Handel, Mendelssohn and contemporary oratorio, alongside orchestral music from the Continent. Visits to London widened that education. Wagner mattered particularly: the chromatic connection between chords, the orchestral recollection of earlier events and the long postponement of a cadence all entered Elgar’s language. His mature scores acquired part of their English character through their subsequent public use.
composer.epithet: A Worcester violinist who made orchestral variations into portraits of friends and the concerto into an argument with memory.
